rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Known material conditions such as parents’ temperament, nourishment, and region shape life, but countless hidden causes remain; unusual cases show our account is incomplete.
rows.anchor: إلا بعض الأسباب العامة البينة التي ليس لها قدر تجاه ما نجهله منها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Good source-material inclines people toward knowledge, sound action, and Paradise; bad dispositions lead to superstition, indulgence, pride, and misery.
rows.anchor: سعادة الإنسان في حياته أعني سعادته في علمه وعمله لها ارتباط تام بطيب مواده الأصلية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These material factors are predispositions, not complete causes: God retains will and can disclose another cause that overcomes them.
rows.anchor: غير أنهما مقتضيان من غير علية تامة، ولله سبحانه المشيئة فيهما والبداء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A subtler account makes happiness and misery stable acts of cognition, which are immaterial and therefore not bounded by the time of bodily motion that produces them.
rows.anchor: السعادة والشقاوة في الإنسان إنما تتحققان بفعلية الإدراك واستقراره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Just as people date created events although God creates each event together with its time, temporal bodily processes accompany cognition without limiting cognition itself.
rows.anchor: الفعل الإلهي غير متقيد بالزمان لأنه موجد مجموع الحادث وزمانه وسائر ما يتقيد به

rows.speaker: الصادق
rows.claim: A report says God made fresh water for the obedient and bitter water for sinners, then mixed them; otherwise believers and unbelievers would reproduce only their own kind.
rows.anchor: عن الصادق عليه السلام قال إن الله عز وجل خلق ماء عذبا فخلق منه أهل طاعته

rows.speaker: الصادق
rows.claim: In Ibn Sinan’s report, water was the first created thing; God blessed the fresh sea for obedience and Paradise, cursed the unresponsive salt sea for disobedience and Hell, then mixed them.
rows.anchor: عن ابن سنان عن الصادق عليه السلام قال سألته عن أول ما خلق الله فقال إن أول ما خلق الله

rows.speaker: الصادق
rows.claim: A further report has God command fresh and salty water to become the origins of Paradise and Hell, then run both over clay, explaining believers arising from unbelievers and vice versa.
rows.anchor: عن عثمان بن عيسى عن بعض أصحابه عنه عليه السلام قال إن الله قال لماء كن عذبا فراتا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author presents these three narrations as examples of many similar reports transmitted from Ali, al-Baqir, al-Sadiq, and others.
rows.anchor: وفي معنى كل من هذه الأحاديث الثلاثة أحاديث كثيرة أخرى مروية عن علي والباقر والصادق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two-seas passage illustrates differences among people despite shared humanity and some shared benefits; the author links the narrations to verses about creation from water.
rows.anchor: وما يستوي البحران هذا عذب فرات سائغ شرابه وهذا ملح أجاج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports about water divide into clay-specific accounts, which reprise differing clay origins, and broader accounts making water the origin of creation and of human happiness or misery.
rows.anchor: وأما الروايات فإنها - كما ترى - في معناها تعود قسمين أحدهما ما يذكر أن الماءين العذب الفرات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clay accounts explain the broader water accounts, and together both clarify earlier reports about primordial clay; the origin of creation in water is deferred for later discussion.
rows.anchor: وثانيهما ما دل على أن الخلقة أعم من خلقة الإنسان وغيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other reports attribute human difference to creation from light and darkness; al-Sadiq’s report says the Imams were made from a novel light rooted in high clay, and Shiite hearts from their substance.
rows.anchor: كما في العلل عن الصادق عليه السلام قال إن الله تبارك وتعالى خلقنا من نور مبتدع من نور سنخ ذلك النور

rows.speaker: الصادق
rows.claim: The continuation says enemies’ hearts were made from Sijjin, while Shiite hearts were made from the substance of their bodies and incline toward them.
rows.anchor: وإن الله تبارك وتعالى خلق قلوب أعدائنا من طينة من سجين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The light-and-darkness reports return to the earlier account of origins in Illiyin and Sijjin; happiness’s clay reveals truth and knowledge, while misery’s clay carries obscurity.
rows.anchor: وهو في الحقيقة راجع إلى ما تقدم من الروايات الدالة على انتهاء الخلقة إلى طينة عليين وطينة سجين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an often calls knowledge and guidance light and faith life, and other reports make prophets, angels, the Preserved Tablet, Pen, Throne, Kursi, and Paradise originate in light.
rows.anchor: وكثيرا ما يسمي القرآن العلم والهدى نورا كما يسمي الإيمان حياة

rows.speaker: الباقر
rows.claim: Al-Baqir tells Ibrahim al-Laythi that at Resurrection God will return each person’s alien spiritual substance and deeds to its true source: the sinner’s to the adversary and the believer’s to the believer.
rows.anchor: عن إبراهيم الليثي عن الباقر عليه السلام في حديث طويل ثم قال أخبرني يا إبراهيم عن الشمس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited report rests on 8:37: at Resurrection God completely separates good from evil, gathers every evil together, and returns effects and deeds to their proper origins.
rows.anchor: ليميز الله الخبيث من الطيب، ويجعل الخبيث بعضه على بعض فيركمه جميعا فيجعله في جهنم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sun-ray comparison portrays an effect as manifesting its cause and remaining attached to its source.
rows.anchor: تمثيل بظاهر الحس على كون الأثر مظهرا لمؤثره مسانخا له قائما به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although transfer of deeds may look unjust, real justice assigns each deed to the essence that matches it; apparent subjects can carry effects whose true source lies elsewhere, like heat in water from the sun or fire.
rows.anchor: وجوب المناسبة والسنخية بين الفاعل وفعله والمؤثر وأثره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses assigning each deed to its doer concern ordinary social responsibility; the inward, malakut judgment returns deeds to the original essence matching them, so the two levels do not conflict.
rows.anchor: فهذا الحكم الباطني الذي يسميه عليه السلام حكما ملكوتيا في طول الحكم الظاهري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because Resurrection exposes hidden realities without concealment, it manifests this inward judgment and returns every result to its true origin.
rows.anchor: وإذا كان يوم القيامة هو اليوم الذي تبلى فيه السرائر وتظهر فيه الحقائق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Barzakh is treated as a continuation of earthly life and remains governed by some worldly conditions; people are still being purified before the final judgment of their complete essence.
rows.anchor: فالحياة البرزخية كأنها من بقايا الحياة الدنيوية محكومة ببعض أحكامها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This explains why disbelievers may be repaid for good deeds in worldly life, while their deeds have no weight in the afterlife and they face only Hell.
rows.anchor: أن الله سبحانه يجازي الكفار جزاء حسناتهم التي أتوا بها في الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Questioning an act asks its agent to show how it matches reality; God’s acts and words are reality itself, while human judgments are derived from the world God creates.
rows.anchor: فلا معنى للسؤال عنه بلم وكيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Questions about events arise from ignorance of their causal chain: knowing each cause, as in a wall falling on Zayd after rain, removes the question of why it happened.
rows.anchor: ولا يقع السؤال إلا على أثر مجهول العلة، وأما الأثر المعلوم العلة فلا يقع عنه سؤال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s and the prophets’ judgments are authorized judgments of inward truth, unlike human judgments based on outward signs; this explains deeds returning to matching natures.
rows.anchor: أي قضاؤه تعالى وقضاء أنبيائه بإذنه فإنه تعالى إنما يقضي ويحكم الحكم الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Makkāʾ means whistling, while makkāʾ can name a strongly whistling Hijazi bird; taṣdiya is clapping. The prayer clause concerns Quraysh and links to the preceding verse as a circumstantial phrase.
rows.anchor: المكاء بضم الميم الصفير، والمكاء بصيغة المبالغة طائر بالحجاز شديد الصفير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The resultative ‘taste the punishment’ completes the warning, and the shift from third-person description to direct address intensifies the rebuke.
rows.anchor: والالتفات في قوله { فذوقوا العذاب } عن الغيبة إلى الخطاب لبلوغ التشديد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If obstruction empties the Kaaba of worship, divine punishment follows; Ali warns that neglecting the House will leave people without respite.
rows.anchor: الله الله في بيت ربكم فإنه إن ترك لم تنظروا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Disbelievers spend to obstruct God’s path, but their efforts waste their wealth, bring regret, and end in defeat; Hell explains why their worldly coalition for evil fails.
rows.anchor: فتضيع الأموال في هذا الطريق فيكون ضيعتها موجبة لتحسرهم، ثم يغلبون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As a Qur’anic prediction after Badr, the spending and regret may point to Uhud and later events, defeat to the conquest of Mecca, and Hell to those who never accept Islam.
rows.anchor: فكأنها تشير إلى ما سيقع من غزوة أحد أو هي وغيرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khabith and tayyib are opposites; distinguishing separates something from what conflicts with it and joins it to what agrees, while piling means stacking parts together.
rows.anchor: والتمييز إخراج الشيء عما يخالفه وإلحاقه بما يوافقه بحيث ينفصل عما يخالفه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse explains why disbelievers’ strenuous campaign against God’s light fails: divine order separates evil from good, gathers evil into Hell, and sends good toward Paradise.
rows.anchor: أن الله سبحانه يميز في هذا النظام الجاري الشر من الخير والخبيث من الطيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The image closely matches the water-and-foam parable: falsehood vanishes while what benefits people remains, expressing the universal law that each branch joins its root.
rows.anchor: والآية تشير إلى قانون كلي إلهي وهو إلحاق فرع كل شيء بأصله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Intihāʾ means stopping because of a prohibition, salaf means what came before, and sunnah means a path or practice; the Prophet is to invite them to stop fighting so earlier crimes may be forgiven.
rows.anchor: الانتهاء الإقلاع عن الشيء لأجل النهي، والسلوف التقدم، والسنة هي الطريقة والسيرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If they persist, God’s established precedent brings destruction and loss, as happened to their predecessors.
rows.anchor: فقد مضت سنة الله في الأولين منهم بالإهلاك والإبادة وخسران السعي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believers receive the counterpart duty: do not relent in establishing the religion and clearing a sound environment for Muslims; fight until persecution ends and religion belongs wholly to God.
rows.anchor: وقاتلوهم حتى لا تكون فتنة ويكون الدين كله لله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the opponents stop, God judges their deeds; if they turn away, believers must continue fighting, trusting God as their patron and fearing nothing.
rows.anchor: فإن انتهوا فإن الله يجازيهم بما يرى من أعمالهم، وإن تولوا عن الانتهاء فأديموا القتال

rows.speaker: القمي
rows.claim: Al-Qummi’s occasion report says the Aws and Khazraj first agreed at al-Aqaba to protect the Prophet and hear the revelation, with Paradise promised as their reward.
rows.anchor: وفي تفسير القمي كان سبب نزولها أنه لما أظهر رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم الدعوة بمكة قدمت عليه الأوس والخزرج

rows.speaker: القمي
rows.claim: Seventy men later pledged to worship God alone and protect Muhammad, his family, and children; the promised rewards included Paradise, Arab rule, and Persian submission.
rows.anchor: فجاء سبعون رجلا من الأوس والخزرج فدخلوا الدار فقال لهم رسول الله

rows.speaker: القمي
rows.claim: Gabriel identified twelve pledge witnesses, nine from Khazraj and three from Aws; Satan alerted Quraysh, prompting an armed response and the Quraysh council at Dar al-Nadwa.
rows.anchor: فأشار إليهم جبرائيل فقال هذا نقيب وهذا نقيب تسعة من الخزرج وثلاثة من الأوس

rows.speaker: القمي
rows.claim: Abu Jahl proposed a lone assassin with ten bloodwits for Muhammad; the Najdi elder rejected this and confinement until death, and the account ends as Quraysh consider exile.
rows.anchor: وسمع رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم النداء فقال للأنصار تفرقوا فقالوا يا رسول الله إن أمرتنا أن نميل عليهم بأسيافنا فعلنا

rows.speaker: القمي
rows.claim: The Prophet said God had not authorized him or the pledge-makers to fight Quraysh; Hamza and Ali stood armed at al-Aqaba and sent them back.
rows.anchor: لم اؤمر بذلك ولم يأذن الله لي في محاربتهم

rows.speaker: القمي
rows.claim: At Dar al-Nadwa Abu Jahl described Muhammad’s former standing and accused him of dividing Quraysh; the Najdi elder rejected a lone assassin and confinement because either would provoke Banu Hashim and allies.
rows.anchor: قال أبو جهل يا معشر قريش إنه لم يكن أحد من العرب أعز منا

rows.speaker: القمي
rows.claim: Quraysh then proposed expelling Muhammad, but the report continues with the Najdi elder’s objection that he could win over the tribes and return with an army.
rows.anchor: قال آخر منهم لا ولكنا نخرجه من بلادنا ونتفرغ لعبادة آلهتنا

rows.speaker: القمي
rows.claim: The Najdi elder said exile would let Muhammad persuade the tribes; he urged a coordinated attack by men from every clan, including Banu Hashim, so blood responsibility would be shared, and Abu Lahab joined.
rows.anchor: يجتمع من كل بطن من بطون قريش فيكون معهم من بني هاشم رجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gabriel informed the Prophet of the plot, and the author says verse 8:30 was revealed about it.
rows.anchor: فأنزل الله عليه في ذلك { وإذ يمكر بك الذين كفروا ليثبتوك أو يقتلوك أو يخرجوك

rows.speaker: القمي
rows.claim: The report connects Quraysh’s whistling and clapping around the Kaaba during their plot to verse 8:35, which the author says was placed after many intervening verses.
rows.anchor: فأنزل الله { وما كان صلاتهم عند البيت إلا مكاء وتصدية } فالمكاء التصفير

rows.speaker: القمي
rows.claim: Ali slept in the Prophet’s bed under his cloak; Gabriel led the Prophet past the sleeping plotters, reciting 36:9, and directed him toward the cave at Mount Thawr.
rows.anchor: وجاء جبرئيل فأخذ بيد رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم فأخرجه على قريش وهم نيام

rows.speaker: القمي
rows.claim: The tracker Abu Karz followed the Prophet’s and Abu Bakr’s footprints to the cave, but a spider’s web and an angelic horseman made the pursuers turn away, after which God permitted the Hijra.
rows.anchor: ولا يزال يقف بهم حتى أوقفهم على باب الغار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A summarized report from Ibn Abbas through Ibn Ishaq and other transmitters instead attributes the collective-killing proposal to Abu Jahl, with the Najdi elder approving it.
rows.anchor: لكن نسب فيه إلى أبي جهل ما نسب في هذه الرواية إلى الشيخ النجدي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports from both Shiite and Sunni routes identify the Najdi elder at Dar al-Nadwa as Satan in disguise.
rows.anchor: وقد روي دخول إبليس عليهم في دار الندوة في زي شيخ نجدي في عدة روايات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other reports identify the third person with Muhammad and Abu Bakr as Hind ibn Abi Hala, the Prophet’s stepson through Khadija.
rows.anchor: فقد ورد في الروايات أن ثالثهما هند بن أبي هالة ربيب رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم وأمه خديجة بنت خويلد

rows.speaker: ابن هند بن أبي هالة
rows.claim: The report says Hind returned to Mecca after guiding the Prophet and Abu Bakr to the cave, then came back with Ali the next night.
rows.anchor: ثم رجع هند إلى مكة

rows.speaker: هند بن أبي هالة
rows.claim: The Prophet passed Quraysh reciting 36:9, joined Abu Bakr and Hind, and reached the cave; Hind returned to Mecca, then later came with Ali to the cave.
rows.anchor: فخرج وهو يقرأ هذه الآية { وجعلنا من بين أيديهم سدا ومن خلفهم سدا فأغشيناهم فهم لا يبصرون }

rows.speaker: هند بن أبي هالة
rows.claim: The Prophet required payment for Abu Bakr’s camels, then gave Ali the purchase money and ordered him to return deposits and debts entrusted to Muhammad by Quraysh and other visitors.
rows.anchor: فقال إني لا آخذهما ولا أحدهما إلا بالثمن

rows.speaker: هند بن أبي هالة
rows.claim: The Prophet charged Ali with protecting Fatima and arranging mounts for himself, the Fatimas, and migrating Hashimites; the report says Khadija’s wealth supplied the money.
rows.anchor: فأمر أن يبتاع رواحل له وللفواطم ومن أزمع الهجرة معه من بني هاشم

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: Ali’s verses recall risking his life in the Prophet’s bed while Muhammad spent three nights safe in the cave; al-Durr al-Manthur also transmits the poem with slight variation through Ali Zayn al-Abidin.
rows.anchor: وقد روى الأبيات عنه عليه السلام بتفاوت يسير في الدر المنثور عن الحاكم عن علي بن الحسين

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر وأبو عبد الله
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet endured severe abuse, including sheep entrails placed on him while prostrating, then saw victory grow from one horseman at Badr to twelve thousand at the conquest.
rows.anchor: عن زرارة وحمران عن أبي جعفر وأبي عبد الله عليهما السلام قوله { خير الماكرين } قال إن رسول الله

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says al-Nadr ibn al-Harith learned Persian rhymed speech and claimed he could produce something like the Qur’an; other reports name al-Nadr as speaker, and he was killed at Badr.
rows.anchor: عن السدي رضي الله عنه قال كان النضر بن الحارث يختلف إلى الحيرة

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك
rows.claim: Anas reports that Abu Jahl challenged God to send stones if Muhammad’s claim were true, and verse 8:33 then declared there would be no punishment while the Prophet was among them or they sought forgiveness.
rows.anchor: عن أنس بن مالك رضي الله عنه قال قال أبو جهل بن هشام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other reports assign that challenge to al-Nadr rather than Abu Jahl; the author says the surrounding context favors this attribution.
rows.anchor: عن سعيد بن جبير وعن ابن جرير عن عطاء

rows.speaker: عطية
rows.claim: Atiyya reads ‘while you are among them’ as protecting Meccan polytheists until the Prophet left, and ‘while they seek forgiveness’ as referring to believers.
rows.anchor: عن عطية رض في قوله { وما كان الله ليعذبهم وأنت فيهم } يعني المشركين حتى يخرجك منهم

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says repentance and admission of sin would make the polytheists believers; their failure to seek forgiveness explains why they can be punished under 8:34.
rows.anchor: عن السدي رض في قوله { وما كان الله معذبهم وهم يستغفرون } يقول لو استغفروا وأقروا

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid interprets the Prophet as being in their midst and seeking forgiveness as accepting Islam.
rows.anchor: عن مجاهد رض في قوله { وما كان الله ليعذبهم وأنت فيهم } قال بين أظهرهم

rows.speaker: أبو مالك
rows.claim: Abu Malik says the verse concerns Mecca’s people, among whom believers were asking forgiveness.
rows.anchor: عن أبي مالك رض { وما كان الله ليعذبهم وأنت فيهم } يعني أهل مكة

rows.speaker: عكرمة والحسن
rows.claim: Ikrima and al-Hasan say the following verse abrogated the promise; they were fought in Mecca and afflicted by famine and siege.
rows.anchor: عن عكرمة والحسن رضي عنهما في قوله { وما كان الله معذبهم وهم يستغفرون } قالا نسختها الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The abrogation reading contradicts the verse’s plain sense and context, apparently to preserve a link with earlier Meccan passages; treating the conquest as punishment is also implausible because it was mercy.
rows.anchor: عدم انطباقها على الآية بظاهرها المؤيد بسياقها ظاهر

rows.speaker: أبو موسى الأشعري
rows.claim: A Tirmidhi report calls the Prophet and seeking forgiveness two safeguards for the community, with forgiveness continuing after his death.
rows.anchor: عن أبي موسى الأشعري رض قال قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says the safeguards report follows from the verse and has parallels from Abu Hurayra, Ibn Abbas, and Ali, but its claim that forgiveness lasts to Resurrection conflicts with the Qur’an’s promised pre-Resurrection punishment.
rows.anchor: وهو أنه لا يلائم ما مر في البيان المتقدم من إيعاد القرآن هذه الأمة بعذاب واقع قبل يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: فضالة بن عبيد
rows.claim: A report from the Prophet says a servant remains safe from God’s punishment as long as he seeks forgiveness.
rows.anchor: عن فضالة بن عبيد رضي الله عنه عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال العبد آمن من عذاب الله ما استغفر الله

rows.speaker: الباقر
rows.claim: Al-Baqir reports the Prophet saying his presence among the people was good for them, while his departure could also benefit them; the next passage explains how.
rows.anchor: عن أبي جعفر عليه السلام قال قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم مقامي بين أظهركم خير لكم

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: Asked how the Prophet’s departure could be beneficial, he says people’s deeds are shown to him every Thursday and Monday: he thanks God for good deeds and seeks forgiveness for bad ones.
rows.anchor: فقال أما مفارقتي لكم خير لكم فإن أعمالكم تعرض علي كل خميس واثنين

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Said ibn Jubayr says Quraysh mocked the Prophet during circumambulation with whistles and clapping, prompting verse 8:35.
rows.anchor: عن سعيد بن جبير رض قال كانت قريش تعارض النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم في الطواف يستهزئون ويصفرون ويصفقون

rows.speaker: نبيط
rows.claim: Nabit, a Companion, says people circumambulated the Sacred House while whistling.
rows.anchor: عن نبيط وكان من الصحابة رض في قوله { وما كان صلاتهم عند البيت } الآية قال كانوا يطوفون

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains makkāʾ as a lark’s call and taṣdiya as birdsong or clapping; two men from Banu Sahm whistled and clapped beside the Prophet to disrupt his prayer.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما إن نافع بن الأزرق قال له أخبرني عن قوله عز وجل { إلا مكاء وتصدية }

rows.speaker: الصادق
rows.claim: Al-Sadiq explains that idolaters were not guardians of the House; only the God-fearing qualify, and their supposed prayer was whistling and clapping.
rows.anchor: عن إبراهيم بن عمر اليماني عمن ذكره عن أبي عبد الله عليه السلام في قول الله { وهم يصدون عن المسجد الحرام

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: After Badr, Quraysh leaders including Abd Allah ibn Rabi‘a, Ikrima, and Safwan asked merchants to fund a war for revenge; Ibn Abbas’s report connects this to the spending verse.
rows.anchor: كما ذكر عن ابن عباس أنزل الله { إن الذين كفروا ينفقون أموالهم ليصدوا عن سبيل الله }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham’s patience explains his gentle promise to his father, while being awwāh—often sighing from fear and hope in God—explains his prayer for forgiveness.
rows.anchor: والأواه هو الكثير التأوه خوفا من ربه وطمعا فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the ban on praying for polytheists, the verse warns believers that God may lead them astray if they fail to avoid what He has clarified as forbidden, including seeking forgiveness for God’s enemies or befriending them.
rows.anchor: ففيه تهديد للمؤمنين بالإضلال بعد الهداية إن لم يتقوا ما بين الله لهم أن يتقوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage expresses a general rule: guidance and blessing continue until people change through ingratitude or transgression, whereupon God removes them.
rows.anchor: من السنة الإلهية أن تستمر على العبد نعمته وهدايته حتى يغير هو ما عنده بالكفران والتعدي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The following verse grounds the ban on loyalty to God’s enemies: God alone truly protects and helps, so believers should direct loyalty only to Him or allies He authorizes.
rows.anchor: لا ولي ولا نصير حقيقة إلا الله سبحانه وقد بينه للمؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God owns the heavens and earth and controls life and death, so He alone governs every affair and is the true patron.
rows.anchor: إن الله سبحانه هو الذي يملك كل شيء وبيده الموت والحياة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rule is general: disavow or do not ally with all enemies of God, not only through prayers for forgiveness but in every form, including idolaters, unbelievers, hypocrites, innovators, and persistent usurers.
rows.anchor: أن الحكم عام وهو وجوب التبري أو حرمة التولي لأعداء الله سواء كان التولي بالاستغفار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hour of hardship is a time when thirst, hunger, extreme heat, or similar trials make life difficult; zaygh means leaving the path, and here it is refusing the Prophet’s command by delaying or abandoning the expedition.
rows.anchor: والزيغ هو الخروج من الطريق والميل عن الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Takhalluf means leaving something behind; rahb means spaciousness, so ‘the earth despite its breadth’ describes their distress even in a wide world.
rows.anchor: والرحب هو السعة التي تقابل الضيق، وبما رحبت أي برحبها فما مصدرية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verses address distinct groups and kinds of repentance—some in the first group had not sinned, while the three laggards had—but the syntax joins them into one statement revealed together.
rows.anchor: وبالجملة الآيتان مختلفتان غرضا ومدلولا غير أن السياق يدل على أنهما مسوقتان لغرض واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The chief purpose is to describe God’s pardon of the three laggards; mention of the Prophet, Emigrants, and Helpers reassures them by placing all groups on equal terms after pardon.
rows.anchor: ولعل الغرض الأصلي بيان توبة الله سبحانه لأولئك الثلاثة المخلفين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated repentance follows an overview-then-detail structure: God’s repentance is first stated for everyone, then specified for each group and finally for the three so that they may repent.
rows.anchor: فليس إلا أن الكلام مسوق على منهج الإجمال والتفصيل ذكر فيه توبته تعالى على الجميع إجمالا
